newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senators agree on tuna-dolphin bill.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senators agree on tuna-dolphin bill.

text.p: U.S. senators announced on Friday they had reached an agreement on legislation to lift the U.S. embargo on tuna caught in huge nets that also may snare dolphins.
But the accord will also bar tuna caught that way from being labeled "dolphin safe" until at least March 1999, when a study on how the practice impacts dolphin populations is completed.

Following the agreement, the Senate is expected to vote next week on the legislation to lift the U.S. embargo, which was sought by Mexico and other countries that fish for tuna in the Eastern Tropical Pacific, where they tend to swim beneath dolphin. The bill should pass easily, Senate aides said.

The House passed its version of the legislation in May that lifted the embargo on tuna caught in encircling nets and allowed cans of that tuna to be branded as dolphin-safe as long as no dolphin deaths were seen by shipboard observers during the catch.

However, after a hard-fought compromise, the Senate version is expected to bar the dolphin-safe label on tuna caught by chasing dolphin and setting nets on top of them until a study on how this fishing practice affects dolphin populations is done in March 1999.
"The label does not change until they can do scientific study that proves that it does not impact the dolphin," a spokesman for California Democrat Sen. Barbara Boxer said.

Currently, any tuna caught using encircling nets set over dolphins cannot be labeled "dolphin-safe." The law was enacted in 1990, following a public outcry over the slaughter of dolphins in tuna fishing.
The proposed change would allow the dolphin-safe label on tuna caught that way, if the study determines that dolphin populations are not significantly reduced by the practice.

The White House has said that unless the label definition were changed, Mexico and other countries would abandon the U.S. market and revert to their former ways that killed hundreds of thousands of dolphins each year.

Opening the U.S. market would reward those countries for taking the time to free dolphin trapped in their nets and reducing dolphin deaths to just a few thousand a year, the administration has said. Under pressure from Mexico, the White House has lobbied hard for the changes.
Boxer, speaking on the Senate floor, said she had 43 other votes to block a measure that would have immediately allowed the dolphin-safe label to include the encircling nets method.
Boxer and Delaware Democratic Sen. Joseph Biden have insisted on the study before allowing the label to be changed.
Senate Commerce Committee Chairman John McCain said the deal was supported by the administration, the fishing industry, labour unions and a number of environmental groups.
"I believe this bill will enable us to successfully implement an international agreement to protect dolphins," McCain, an Arizona Republican, said in a statement.

The issue has divided wildlife advocates, with some saying dropping the embargo and the label definition is the only way to get Mexico and the other countries to continue to take the time and effort to free dolphins trapped in the nets.

But others say using speed boats and helicopters to chase dolphin -- and the tuna below them -- into encircling nets is inherently cruel to dolphins, causes injuries, trauma and shortened life-spans, and should not be sanctioned.
